It's a good page. The data is right and most of its conclusions hold up when I recompute them. I'd keep its headline ("the S&P is tracking the 2000 top, the tech mania is not"), with two small fixes and one caveat.

## Checking the data
- **Prices:** the daily series built into the page match Yahoo's closes for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100. For example: 1,527.46 on 24 Mar 2000, 7,818.93 on 6 Oct 2026, and 4,704.73 for the Nasdaq-100 on 27 Mar 2000. Only the last point differs, because it's intraday.
- **Table:** rebuilding it from the page's own data gives the same numbers:

| | S&P 2000 | S&P 2026 | Nasdaq-100 2000 | Nasdaq-100 2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 29 sessions after the peak | −6.2% | −5.2% | −25.1% | −12.8% |
| Distance above 200-day average | 11.3% | 8.1% | 55.8% | 13.4% |
| 3-month volatility | 24.3% | 11.1% | 47.0% | 18.6% |

- **Two small fixes:**
  - 29 sessions after 24 Mar 2000 is **5 May**, not 4 May. On 4 May the S&P was down 7.7%.
  - For the Nasdaq-100, 29 sessions after its 27 Mar peak is 8 May. The table header labels both as 4 May.

## Its best-fit match is better than I thought
The page says today's 4-year S&P path most resembles the period ending 4 May 2000, with a correlation of 0.985. My first instinct was that any two rising markets correlate that well. To check, I compared the last 1,008 sessions with every 4-year window since 1950, sampled weekly: 3,464 windows in all.

- **Rank:** the early-May-2000 window is **the best match of all 3,464**. Only 6% of windows even reach 0.95. So the shape match is unusual.
- **The caveat:** daily returns in the two windows correlate at about **0.03**. What repeats is the overall arc (a dip, a long rally, then a rollover), not the day-to-day path.

The next-closest matches show what that arc has usually led to:

| Window ending | Correlation | S&P over the next 12 months | Worst point in those 12 months |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 May 2000 | 0.985 | −10.1% | −21.7% |
| 7 Jul 1999 | 0.976 | +3.6% | −10.6% |
| 11 Aug 2015 | 0.971 | +4.4% | −12.2%
